title: The Izbicer and free choice
hookLine: the Izbicer taught that God's will can hide even in human mistakes
carry: hidden will looking back, free choice looking forward
tomorrow: who keeps teaching when every light goes out?

lines: THE WRONG EXIT, THE RIGHT DINER.
cards: Somebody misreads a map, takes the wrong exit, and ends up at the diner where they meet the person they'll marry. Families love telling that kind of story.
A Hasidic teacher built a whole way of seeing on it: Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izbica, known as the Izbicer, in his book Mei HaShiloach. His answer to the question is yes.
God's will can hide even inside a human mistake. Not everyone in the tradition agrees, and the disagreement is worth hearing out.

teach.b: Here's the Izbicer's view. At its root, everything is in God's hands, even what people do wrong. The Torah's stories show it.

Judah and Tamar is a tangled, shameful episode, and from it comes the line of King David. In his reading, a person can act with full force, even stumble, and later find that a hidden will was moving inside it all along.
That brings comfort: no mistake is outside God's reach. But he doesn't say anything goes.
Here and now, a person still has to act by the Torah's law; the hidden will shows itself only afterward, looking back. Now the other voice.

teach.h: FREE CHOICE, GIVEN TO EVERY PERSON.
teach.b: Maimonides, in his laws of repentance, says free choice is given to every person: anyone can become righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam, and nobody forces them.
Without real choice, he argues, commandments and repair would make no sense.
The Talmud has a line that sits between them: everything is in the hands of heaven, except the fear of heaven. Your reverence, your choosing, is yours.

teach.h: HIDDEN WILL LOOKING BACK, FREE CHOICE LOOKING FORWARD.
teach.b: The best case for Maimonides is responsibility: if the mistake was God's will, why apologize? The best case for the Izbicer is mercy: if God can hide inside the mistake, despair loses its grip. Both are inside Judaism.
Both keep the law. One looks at the moment from before, the other from after.

how: The Izbicer's Mei HaShiloach is studied in Hasidic and other circles alongside classic works on free will such as Maimonides' laws of repentance, and the tension between them is a frequent topic of Jewish study and debate.

o: any wish comes true if God wills it to happen
God's will can hide even inside human mistakes
God's plan is written down in a secret book

games.q: two views of the same moment — tap the pairs.
p: God's will hides even in mistakes
free choice is given to every person
all in heaven's hands but the fear of heaven
from a tangle comes David's line

s: the Izbicer taught that since all is God's will, the law no longer matters
a person must still act by the Torah's law; the hidden will shows only looking back.
Maimonides says anyone can become righteous like Moses
free choice is given to every person, and nobody forces them.
Judaism has one settled answer on free will and God's will
the Izbicer and Maimonides look from after and from before; both are inside the tradition.

games.q: a friend says: 'if God's will hides inside mistakes, then nobody is responsible for anything.' you want to give the Izbicer his best answer. what is it?
o: the hidden will is seen only looking back; right now, you still act by the law.
she's right, so there's no reason to apologize for anything you've done.
mistakes are never part of God's will at all; only good deeds are.
games.why: the Izbicer keeps the law in force here and now. the hidden will is a comfort for afterward, not an excuse for before.

practice: For the sit, let the sounds around you come without choosing them: a car, a fan, a voice through the wall. When one surprises you, don't call it good or bad.
Let it be part of a moment you didn't plan, and stay with it until the next sound arrives.

wordCard.voice: Hidden will everywhere: the Izbicer's teaching that God's will can hide even inside human mistakes, seen only looking back.

orig.note: Hebrew: the waters of Shiloah (Isaiah 8:6), the title of the Izbicer's book.

carryVoice: Keep it close: hidden will looking back, free choice looking forward. Be well.

sources.ref: Mei HaShiloach (Rabbi Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izbica), on Vayeshev (Judah and Tamar) and elsewhere: all is in God's hands; the hidden will revealed afterward
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Repentance 5:1–4 (free choice; righteous like Moses or wicked like Jeroboam)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 33b (everything is in the hands of heaven except the fear of heaven)
